'''Michael Spencer Waterman''' (born June 28, 1942) is a University Professor Emeritus at the [[University of Southern California|University of Southern California (USC)]], where he held the USC Associates Chair in Natural Sciences and was a professor of [[Biology|biological sciences]], [[computer science]], and [[mathematics]].<ref name="Michael_Waterman-1">{{Cite web |title=Michael S Waterman |url=https://dornsife.usc.edu/msw/ |access-date=2026-11-02 |website=Michael Waterman |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2012-02-10 |title=Ray Irani, Michael Waterman Elected to NAE |url=https://dornsife.usc.edu/news/stories/ray-irani-michael-waterman-elected-to-nae/ |access-date=2026-11-02 |website=USC Dornsife News |language=en-US}}</ref> His research has focused on the analysis of DNA, RNA, and protein sequences.<ref name="Michael_Waterman-1" /> He previously held positions at [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]] and [[Idaho State University]].<ref name="Michael_Waterman-1" />

==Education and early life==
Waterman grew up near [[Bandon, Oregon]],<ref name=getting/> and earned a bachelor's degree in Mathematics from [[Oregon State University]], followed by a [[PhD]] in [[statistics]] and [[probability]] from [[Michigan State University]] in 1969.<ref name="msu1969"/><ref name=phd>{{cite thesis |degree=PhD |first=Michael Smith|last=Waterman |title=Some Ergodic Properties of Multi-Dimensional F-Expansions |publisher=Michigan State University |date=1969 |oclc=25799203 |id={{ProQuest|302449931}}}} {{subscription required}}</ref>

==Research and career==
Waterman is one of the founders and current leaders in the area of [[computational biology]]. He focuses on applying mathematics, statistics, and computer science techniques to various problems in [[molecular biology]]. His work has contributed to some of the most widely used tools in the field. In particular, the [[Smith-Waterman algorithm]] (developed with [[Temple F. Smith]]) is the basis for many [[sequence alignment]] programs.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Smith | first1 = T. | last2 = Waterman | first2 = M. S. | author-link2 = Michael Waterman| title = Identification of common molecular subsequences | doi = 10.1016/0022-2836(81)90087-5 | journal = [[Journal of Molecular Biology]] | volume = 147 | issue = 1 | pages = 195–197 | year = 1981 | pmid =  7265238}}</ref> In 1988, Waterman and [[Eric Lander]] published a landmark paper describing a mathematical model for fingerprint mapping.<ref>{{Cite journal
| last1 = Lander | first1 = E. S.
| author-link1 = Eric Lander
| last2 = Waterman | first2 = M. S.
| author-link2 = Michael Waterman
| title = Genomic mapping by fingerprinting random clones: A mathematical analysis
| journal = Genomics
| volume = 2
| issue = 3
| pages = 231–239
| year = 1988
| pmid = 3294162
| doi = 10.1016/0888-7543(88)90007-9
}}</ref> This work formed one of the theoretical cornerstones for many of the later DNA mapping and sequencing projects, especially the [[Human Genome Project]]. A 1995 paper by Idury and Waterman introduced Eulerian-[[De Bruijn sequence]] assembly which is widely used in next-generation sequencing projects.<ref name="IduryWaterman1995">{{cite journal|last1=Idury|first1=Ramana M.|last2=Waterman|first2=Michael S.|title=A New Algorithm for DNA Sequence Assembly|journal=[[Journal of Computational Biology]]|volume=2|issue=2|year=1995|pages=291–306|issn=1066-5277|doi=10.1089/cmb.1995.2.291|pmid=7497130|url=http://dornsife.usc.edu/assets/sites/516/docs/papers/msw_papers/msw-128.pdf}}</ref>

With [[Pavel A. Pevzner]] (a former [[postdoctoral researcher]] in his lab), he began the international conference [[Research in Computational Molecular Biology|Research in Computational Molecular Biology (RECOMB)]],<ref>{{cite web |url=http://recomb.org/ |title= The RECOMB conference series|website=recomb.org|author=Anon|year=2017}}</ref> and he is a founding editor of the ''[[Journal of Computational Biology]]''. Waterman also authored one of the earliest textbooks in the field: ''Introduction to Computational Biology''.<ref>{{cite book |author1=Waterman, Michael R. |author2=Waterman, M. S. |title=Introduction to computational biology: maps, sequences and genomes |publisher=Chapman & Hall |location=London |year=1995 |isbn=978-0-412-99391-6 }}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
With [[Cyrus Chothia]] and [[David Haussler]], Waterman was awarded the 2015 [[Dan David Prize]] for his contributions to the field of [[bioinformatics]].<ref name=dan-david-prize /> He was awarded an [[Honorary Doctorate]] from [[Tel Aviv University]]  in 2011,{{citation needed|date=March 2017}} an [[Honorary Doctorate]] from the [[University of Southern Denmark]] in 2013,{{citation needed|date=March 2017}} and an [[Honorary Doctorate]] from [[Oregon State University]] in 2024. 

Waterman has been a member of the US [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]  since 1995,{{citation needed|date=March 2017}} a member of the US [[National Academy of Engineering]] since 2012,{{citation needed|date=March 2017}} a member of the  [[Chinese Academy of Sciences]] since 2013,{{citation needed|date=March 2017}} and a member of the US [[National Academy of Sciences]] since 2001.{{citation needed|date=March 2017}} He has been an academician of the  [[French Academy of Sciences]] since 2005.{{citation needed|date=March 2017}}

Waterman was elected an [[ISCB Fellow]] in 2009 by the [[International Society for Computational Biology]]<ref name=fellows/> and was awarded their [[ISCB Senior Scientist Award]] in 2006.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Maisel |first=Merry |date=2006-08-04 |title=ISCB Honors Michael S. Waterman and Mathieu Blanchette |journal=PLOS Computational Biology |language=en |publisher=Public Library of Science |volume=2 |issue=8 |article-number=e105 |doi=10.1371/journal.pcbi.0020105 |doi-access=free |issn=1553-7358 |pmc=1526462 |bibcode=2006PLSCB...2..105M }}</ref>

==Personal life==
Waterman has written a memoir, ''Getting Outside'',<ref name=getting>{{cite book|first=Michael|last=Waterman|year=2016|isbn=978-1-5309-2934-4|title=Getting Outside: A Far-Western Childhood|publisher=CreateSpace Independent Publishing Platform}}</ref> of a childhood spent on an isolated livestock ranch on the southern coast of Oregon in the mid-20th century.
